questions.stem: Which description correctly pairs a force with where it acts?

options.text: Covalent bonds act within a single molecule
options.explanation: Shared electron pairs link atoms inside one molecule, which is the intramolecular setting.

options.text: Hydrogen bonds act within a single molecule
options.explanation: Hydrogen bonding links neighbouring molecules, never atoms inside one molecule.

options.text: Induced dipole forces act within the nucleus
options.explanation: Nuclear forces are outside the chemist's classification entirely.

options.text: Intermolecular forces join two atoms into a new molecule
options.explanation: Joining atoms into a molecule is covalent bonding, the intramolecular job.

questions.stem: Which set lists the three intermolecular force types?

options.text: London, metallic, van der Waals
options.explanation: Metallic bonding does not appear in the intermolecular trio.

options.text: Induced dipole-dipole, permanent dipole-dipole, hydrogen bonding
options.explanation: These are exactly the three between-molecule attractions in the strength ladder.

options.text: Ionic, covalent, metallic
options.explanation: Those are the three intramolecular bond classes, not between-molecule forces.

options.text: Single, double, triple
options.explanation: Those grade covalent bond order inside molecules.

questions.stem: Roughly how strong is one hydrogen bond compared with a covalent bond?

options.text: Exactly equal
options.explanation: Equality would erase the melting and boiling point patterns the ladder explains.

options.text: About one thousandth as strong
options.explanation: That understates the hydrogen bond badly.

options.text: About one tenth as strong
options.explanation: The hydrogen bond reaches roughly a tenth of a covalent bond's strength, which still beats every other intermolecular pull.

options.text: About ten times stronger
options.explanation: Nothing between molecules outmuscles a covalent bond by that margin.

questions.stem: Which statement about the strength ladder is correct?

options.text: Permanent dipole-dipole is the weakest type
options.explanation: Permanent dipoles outpull induced ones at equal size, so they cannot be last.

options.text: Hydrogen bonding is weaker than induced dipole-dipole
options.explanation: Hydrogen bonding tops the between-molecule ladder.

options.text: All three types share identical strength
options.explanation: The whole point of the ladder is that the ranks differ.

options.text: Induced dipole-dipole is the weakest of the three intermolecular types
options.explanation: Fleeting dipoles give the gentlest attraction, sitting at the ladder's foot.

questions.stem: A single, double or co-ordinate bond belongs to which family?

options.text: Intramolecular forces
options.explanation: All of those bond orders are covalent links inside one molecule.

options.text: Intermolecular forces
options.explanation: Between-molecule attractions never come in single, double or co-ordinate varieties.

options.text: Hydrogen bonding
options.explanation: Hydrogen bonding is one intermolecular type, unrelated to bond order.

options.text: Nuclear attractions
options.explanation: Nuclear forces hold nuclei together, not molecules.

questions.stem: State the difference between intramolecular and intermolecular forces, with one example of each.
questions.modelAnswer: Intramolecular forces act inside one molecule, for example the covalent bonds sharing electron pairs; intermolecular forces act between neighbouring molecules, for example hydrogen bonding between water molecules.

questions.stem: Name the three intermolecular force types in increasing strength order.
questions.modelAnswer: Induced dipole-dipole comes first, permanent dipole-dipole second, and hydrogen bonding third as the strongest between-molecule attraction.

questions.stem: Explain why boiling a molecular liquid never breaks its covalent bonds.
questions.modelAnswer: Boiling only has to overcome the intermolecular attractions between molecules, which are far weaker than the covalent bonds inside each molecule, so the molecules separate intact and no covalent bond snaps.

questions.stem: A hydrogen bond carries one tenth of a covalent bond's strength. If a C-H covalent bond stores 413 kJ per mole, estimate the hydrogen bond energy per mole.
questions.modelAnswer: One tenth of 413 kJ per mole is 41.3 kJ per mole, so the hydrogen bond ranks far below the covalent bond yet still leads the intermolecular ladder.

questions.stem: What creates a temporary dipole in a non-polar molecule?

options.text: Its nucleus shifts between the atoms
options.explanation: Nuclei stay essentially fixed while electrons do the moving.

options.text: Its electron cloud drifts and piles up unevenly on one side
options.explanation: Constant cloud motion concentrates charge momentarily, producing the fleeting dipole.

options.text: Its covalent bonds snap open
options.explanation: Bond breaking is far too energetic and unrelated to fleeting dipoles.

options.text: A permanent charge separation built into the structure
options.explanation: A permanent separation would make the molecule polar, contradicting the premise.

questions.stem: Which statement about induced dipole-dipole forces is correct?

options.text: They require hydrogen attached to fluorine
options.explanation: That condition describes hydrogen bonding instead.

options.text: They appear only in the solid state
options.explanation: The forces operate in every physical state.

options.text: They exist between all atoms and molecules
options.explanation: Every electron cloud can flicker, so every pair feels this attraction.

options.text: They exist only between non-polar molecules
options.explanation: Polar molecules also carry induced contributions on top of their permanent ones.

questions.stem: Why does the induced dipole in the neighbour form at all?

options.text: The neighbour copies the dipole by convention
options.explanation: Copying is not a physical mechanism.

options.text: Covalent bonds stretch across the gap
options.explanation: No shared pair bridges separate molecules here.

options.text: Gravity pulls the heavier end round
options.explanation: Gravitational effects are negligible in molecular attraction.

options.text: The temporary dipole's electric field distorts the neighbour's electron cloud
options.explanation: Charge asymmetry nearby polarises the adjacent cloud, inducing the matching dipole.

questions.stem: Propanone boils higher than butane even though both carry the same electron count. Why?

options.text: Propanone is polar, so its permanent dipole-dipole forces beat butane's induced ones
options.explanation: At equal electrons the induced contribution matches, so polarity decides the winner.

options.text: Butane has more electrons than propanone
options.explanation: The comparison fixes the electron count as equal.

options.text: Propanone has hydrogen bonds
options.explanation: Propanone's oxygen has no attached hydrogen, so no hydrogen bonding occurs.

options.text: Butane is polar
options.explanation: Butane's symmetric hydrocarbon skeleton leaves it non-polar.

questions.stem: Why are induced dipoles only temporary?

options.text: Covalent bonds drain the dipole
options.explanation: Nothing drains a dipole through a bond.

options.text: The electron clouds never stop moving
options.explanation: Ceaseless cloud motion keeps remaking and erasing the charge asymmetry.

options.text: The molecules stop vibrating in solids
options.explanation: Vibration persists in every state.

options.text: Heat destroys the dipoles permanently
options.explanation: The flicker is intrinsic, not a temperature artefact.

questions.stem: Describe how a temporary dipole induces a dipole on a neighbouring molecule.
questions.modelAnswer: The electron cloud drifts to one side giving a temporary dipole, whose electric field pulls the neighbour's cloud into a matching induced dipole, and the opposite ends then attract.

questions.stem: State the relative strength of permanent dipole-dipole and induced dipole-dipole forces for small molecules of equal electron count.
questions.modelAnswer: Permanent dipole-dipole forces are stronger than induced dipole-dipole forces when the molecules are small and carry the same number of electrons.

questions.stem: Explain why larger electron counts raise boiling points through induced forces alone.
questions.modelAnswer: More electrons make cloud distortions bigger and more frequent, so the temporary dipoles are larger and the induced attractions stronger, which raises the energy needed to separate molecules.

questions.stem: Propanone needs more energy to separate its molecules than butane at equal electron count. If butane's intermolecular energy per mole is 22 kJ and polarity roughly doubles the pull, estimate propanone's figure.
questions.modelAnswer: Doubling 22 kJ per mole gives about 44 kJ per mole for propanone, the premium the permanent dipoles charge over the induced baseline.

questions.stem: Which elements must bond to hydrogen for hydrogen bonding to occur?

options.text: Sodium, potassium or calcium
options.explanation: These are metals, not the electronegative partners required.

options.text: Chlorine, bromine or iodine
options.explanation: Halogen bonds to hydrogen stay polar but fall short of hydrogen bonding strength.

options.text: Oxygen, nitrogen or fluorine
options.explanation: Only these highly electronegative atoms polarise the hydrogen enough for the link.

options.text: Carbon, sulfur or phosphorus
options.explanation: None of these pull electron density hard enough from hydrogen.

questions.stem: What does the hydrogen in a hydrogen bond reach toward?

options.text: The covalent bond of the neighbour
options.explanation: The link forms to a lone pair, not into a bond.

options.text: The neighbour's nucleus
options.explanation: Direct nuclear contact is not the mechanism.

options.text: Another hydrogen atom
options.explanation: Hydrogen-to-hydrogen contact is not hydrogen bonding.

options.text: A lone pair on an oxygen, nitrogen or fluorine of a neighbouring molecule
options.explanation: The exposed positive hydrogen links to a lone pair facing it.

questions.stem: Why does a water molecule form two hydrogen bonds?

options.text: Its oxygen carries two lone pairs
options.explanation: Each lone pair can face one delta-positive hydrogen of a neighbour.

options.text: It has two hydrogen atoms only
options.explanation: Two hydrogens make it a donor, but the count of links formed is set by the lone pairs.

options.text: It is the smallest molecule available
options.explanation: Size does not set the bonding count.

options.text: Its hydrogen atoms are unusually negative
options.explanation: The hydrogens are delta-positive, not negative.

questions.stem: Which ranking of hydrogen bonding is correct?

options.text: Equal in strength to permanent dipole-dipole forces
options.explanation: Hydrogen bonding is a strengthened sub-case, not an equal.

options.text: Strongest intermolecular attraction, yet weaker than any covalent bond
options.explanation: It tops the between-molecule ladder while staying about a tenth of a covalent bond.

options.text: Stronger than covalent bonds
options.explanation: Nothing between molecules beats the bonds inside them.

options.text: Weaker than induced dipole-dipole forces
options.explanation: Hydrogen bonding sits at the top, not the bottom.

questions.stem: Why does the hydrogen become strongly positive in an O-H bond?

options.text: Oxygen repels the hydrogen nucleus
options.explanation: Repulsion is not the source of polarity.

options.text: The bond is ionic from the start
options.explanation: An O-H bond is polar covalent, not fully ionic.

options.text: Oxygen pulls the shared electrons toward itself
options.explanation: High electronegativity drains density from hydrogen, exposing its positive character.

options.text: Hydrogen donates its proton
options.explanation: The proton stays covalently held; only electron density shifts.

questions.stem: State the two requirements for hydrogen bonding between two molecules.
questions.modelAnswer: One molecule must carry hydrogen covalently bonded to oxygen, nitrogen or fluorine, and the other molecule must present a lone pair on such an atom for the hydrogen to reach.

questions.stem: Give the strength ladder from weakest to strongest for induced, permanent and hydrogen-bonded attractions.
questions.modelAnswer: Induced dipole-dipole is weakest, permanent dipole-dipole sits in the middle, and hydrogen bonding is the strongest intermolecular attraction.

questions.stem: Explain why hydrogen bonding counts as a special case of permanent dipole-dipole attraction.
questions.modelAnswer: Both attractions run between fixed positive and negative ends of polar molecules; hydrogen bonding is the extreme version where electronegative atoms concentrate so much charge on hydrogen that a lone pair completes an unusually strong dipole link.

questions.stem: Ethanoic acid pairs up through two hydrogen bonds per dimer. If one hydrogen bond is worth 25 kJ per mole, how much extra energy does forming the double bridge contribute per mole of dimer?
questions.modelAnswer: Two hydrogen bonds at 25 kJ per mole each give 50 kJ per mole, which is why the dimer survives even in the gas phase.
